lesson.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specAnchors.text: understand that covalent bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between two nuclei and the shared pair of electrons between them, based on the evidence: i the physical properties of giant atomic structures ii electron density maps for simple molecules

primer.text: Covalent bonds pool electrons rather than transfer them: two nuclei, one shared pair, stability from a double attraction. Bond polarity grades the sharing by electronegativity difference, and the octet rule bends at both ends - period-3 expansion and boron's deficiency. This note runs from the hydrogen molecule's charge cloud to simple and giant covalent lattices.

modules.title: Sharing instead of transferring
modules.opening: Covalent bonding joins two non-metals not by handing electrons over but by holding them together: both nuclei attract the same outer-shell pair, two atomic orbitals overlap into a molecular orbital, and the pair sits more stable in the two-nucleus pull than under one nucleus alone. Drawn as H-H, the bond is best imagined as a moving charge cloud rather than a fixed pair of dots.
keyPoints: Covalent bonding occurs between two non-metal atoms.
The bond is the electrostatic attraction between the two nuclei and their shared outer-shell electrons.
No electrons transfer; they are shared, with two atomic orbitals overlapping into a molecular orbital.
Sharing is stabilising because two nuclei attract the pair more strongly than one nucleus alone.
Bonding electrons are best regarded as constantly moving charge clouds, not fixed positions.

low.restatement: Two non-metals each park an electron into a joint cloud between them; both nuclei tug on that cloud, and the shared tug is what glues the pair together.
low.analogy: Two neighbours each holding one end of the same rope: neither owns it outright, but the shared tension binds them together.
low.examPointer: The one-line definition to memorise: electrostatic attraction between the nuclei and the shared pair of electrons.

medium.restatement: Orbital overlap converts two atomic orbitals into one molecular orbital whose electron density concentrates between the nuclei; the pair's stability rises because each electron now feels the pull of two nuclei at once.
medium.analogy: A hammock slung between two posts sags to its lowest, most comfortable point in the middle - electron density settles between two nuclei the same way.
medium.examPointer: When asked why sharing happens, quote the double attraction: two nuclei on one pair beats one nucleus on one pair.

modules.title: Polar bonds and the octet's edges
modules.opening: Sharing is not always equal. Identical atoms split the pair symmetrically - Cl2 is nonpolar - but a more electronegative partner drags the density its way, giving HCl delta charges and an asymmetric distribution. The eight-electron rule bends at both edges too: period-3 centres expand past eight, and boron centres fall short at six.
keyPoints: Equal electronegativities make a covalent bond nonpolar, as in Cl2.
Different electronegativities make the bond polar, drawing electrons toward the more electronegative atom.
In a polar bond the charge centres do not coincide: the delta-negative and delta-positive ends separate.
The greater the electronegativity difference, the more polar the bond, approaching ionic character.
Period-3 atoms can expand past eight electrons; boron compounds can be electron deficient at six.

low.restatement: Identical atoms share fairly; a greedier atom pulls the pair closer, leaving slightly charged ends. Eight electrons is the usual cap, but big atoms can hold more and boron holds fewer.
low.analogy: A tug-of-war between equal teams stays centred; a stronger team drags the rope - and the usual team-size rule bends for giant or short rosters.
low.examPointer: Attach the delta signs correctly: delta-negative sits on the more electronegative atom, delta-positive on the other.

medium.restatement: Polarity is unequal sharing quantified: the electronegativity difference displaces the negative charge centre from the positive one, growing with the difference toward the ionic limit; octet flexibility follows orbital availability - accessible d-orbitals expand period-3 shells, and boron's three valence electrons leave an unfilled orbital.
medium.analogy: A shared blanket pulled by two sleepers of different strength: the stronger one ends up with more blanket, and the 'eight-square' bed rule simply does not fit every sleeper.
medium.examPointer: Quote electron counts for the exceptions: ten around P in PCl5, twelve around S in SF6, six around B in BF3.

modules.title: Simple and giant covalent structures
sourceHeadings: Covalent bonding & simple covalent lattice structures
Covalent bonding & giant covalent lattice structures
modules.opening: The same bond builds two very different worlds. Small molecules - water, nitrogen - hold a fixed atom count and melt easily because only weak intermolecular forces sit between the units. Giant covalent lattices wire countless atoms together with strong covalent bonds, so they melt ferociously high and split into hard diamond-like or soft graphite-like characters depending on where the weak spots sit.
keyPoints: Simple molecules such as H2O and N2 contain fixed numbers of covalently bonded atoms.
Simple covalent lattices melt and boil low because weak intermolecular forces need little energy to break.
Simple covalent compounds rarely conduct: no charged particles exist unless water reaction makes ions, as with HCl.
Giant covalent lattices melt and boil very high because countless strong covalent bonds link the whole structure.
Giant structures can be hard (diamond, silicon(IV) oxide) or soft (graphite, weak between layers).

low.restatement: Little molecules part easily - only weak glue between them - so they melt low and do not conduct. Endless covalent networks take huge energy to break, melting high, and their hardness depends on whether weak layers lurk inside.
low.analogy: A bowl of marbles scatters at a push; a welded steel mesh fights the crowbar - and if the mesh is stacked in slick sheets, it shears soft.
low.examPointer: Conductivity answers hinge on charged particles: name the delocalised electrons in graphite and their absence in diamond.

medium.restatement: Melting temperature reports the weakest link: intermolecular forces for molecular solids, covalent bonds for networks - hence the two regimes differ by hundreds of degrees. Conductivity then demands mobile charge, which molecular solids lack (unless water generates ions) and only layered networks supply.
medium.analogy: Tearing a stack of paper versus sawing a welded frame: the stack fails at its lowest energy path, the frame at its strongest bond.
medium.examPointer: Buckminsterfullerene is the boundary case: a big molecule with high melting points and trapped delocalised electrons that still cannot conduct between molecules.

glossary.definition: The combined orbital formed when two atomic orbitals overlap in a covalent bond, housing the shared pair.
The region of constantly moving electron density that represents a bonding pair.
A covalent bond between atoms of different electronegativity whose shared electrons sit closer to one atom, giving delta charges.
Describing a central atom with fewer than eight outer electrons, such as boron in BF3.
